title: PGA Tour Revamping Fan Code of Conduct Amid Sports Betting Concerns (August 31, 2026)
dek: The PGA Tour is implementing security measures and training programs for the 2027 season in response to player concerns about betting-related fan interference during play. The Tour cited less than 5% of ejections in 2026 as betting-related but stated even one incident is unacceptable, leading to new volunteer ambassador programs and online harassment monitoring.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: PGA Tour senior VP Andy Levinson stated the Tour is concerned about fans with money on the line attempting to impact competition, prompting an ambassador program to train volunteers to identify and report disruptive behavior.
bottom_line: The Tour's ambassador training and online monitoring programs debut for 2027; whether they reduce betting-related incidents below the less-than-5% threshold reported in 2026 will be the early measure of effectiveness. The Tour's continued hold on prediction market partnerships suggests caution will persist until regulatory clarity emerges.
body:
The PGA Tour is deploying new security measures and fan-monitoring programs for the 2027 season to address player concerns about betting-related spectator interference during competitive play. The move marks a direct response to incidents in 2026 where fans with financial stakes in outcomes attempted to disrupt golfers on the course.
PGA Tour senior VP of tournament administration Andy Levinson stated at the Tour Championship, per Front Office Sports: "We are concerned about fans interacting with our players in a negative manner, and certainly the potential for fans to try to impact the competition in some way."
The Tour's new framework includes a volunteer ambassador program, which Levinson described as "a group of volunteers that is being trained to be amongst the crowds and look for certain types of behavior and then notify security." The Tour is also creating programs to track and monitor online commentary from fans about players they have bet on, addressing harassment that may originate on course or migrate online.
PGA Tour VP of gaming Scott Warfield told Front Office Sports that less than 5% of ejections at PGA Tour events in 2026 stemmed from sports betting-related incidents, but framed even that small number as unacceptable. "One is one too many for us," Warfield said, "and it's why we spent the summer talking to players getting their feedback on this, leading to some of the stuff we're looking at for 2027 with the tracking of harassing comments that usually start on the course, go online, or vice versa."
At the WM Phoenix Open in February, a content creator paid a fan $100 to yell during a golfer's backswing, according to Front Office Sports.
Levinson acknowledged practical limits to enforcement: "If you've got 10,000 people standing around a green and somebody decides to blurt something out, those things are really hard to control. So, we do rely on decorum a little bit at golf tournaments. In some markets we've seen that deteriorate."
The Tour has opted not to partner with prediction markets as of 2026, and players are prohibited from signing sponsorships with such platforms. Warfield stated, per Front Office Sports: "We'll get in when we're ready and when it's right for our members. It wasn't in 2026; we'll see what it is in 2027." The Tour cited regulatory uncertainty as a factor, noting ongoing lawsuits over whether prediction market contracts constitute legal financial trades or illegal sports bets. The MLB and NHL have partnered with prediction markets, the USTA signed Kalshi as the exclusive prediction market for the US Open, but the NFL and NBA have not yet done so.
